title: the mudras
hook: a raised open palm on a temple image, and a lowered one beneath it: two hands that speak first

segments.voice: Yesterday the mudras gave the hand a job: steering the breath, one nostril, then the other. Did your hand find its place at the nose? Now the hands turn around and face you. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

A crossing guard steps into the road and lifts one hand, palm out, fingers up. The cars stop. Nobody says anything. The hand says it all. Now stand in front of an image of Shiva as the dancer, ringed in flame. Among his hands, one is raised, open, palm toward you, fingers up. Almost the crossing guard's hand. But it isn't saying stop. It's saying something gentler. So far the mudras have been things a practitioner does. Today, two mudras you don't make. You receive them.
screen: `ONE RAISED PALM STOPS THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE SAME PALM ON SHIVA.` → `A MUDRA YOU RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: That raised, open palm is called abhaya mudra. Abhaya means fearlessness, the absence of fear. The gesture says: do not be afraid. On some images there's a second hand to look for, lowered, palm open toward you, fingers pointing down, as if letting something fall into your hands. That one is varada mudra, the gesture of giving, of granting what is asked. In some paintings of Lakshmi, coins pour from that lowered palm. One hand lifts the fear. The other hand gives. Now open the Bhagavad Gita to its sixteenth chapter. Krishna lists the qualities of a person whose nature leans toward the divine, and the list begins with one word: abhayam, fearlessness. Then purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge, giving, self-control. Fearlessness opens the list. So when a devotee stands before an image with that hand raised, the very quality the Gita names at the head of its list is being held out to them. People read the gesture in more than one way. Some hear a promise: the god protects, there is nothing to fear here. Some hear an invitation: this is a quality meant to grow in the one who looks. The palm holds both readings at once. One more detail: the same raised palm and the same lowered, giving hand also appear on Buddhist and Jain images, each tradition reading them in its own way. A shared language of hands. Which turns the mudras around. They aren't only something you form in a quiet room. They are also something offered to you. You stand in front of a hand, and it speaks first.
screen: `ABHAYA: THE PALM THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.` · `VARADA: THE LOWERED PALM THAT GIVES.` · `GITA 16: THE LIST OPENS WITH FEARLESSNESS.` · `A PROMISE, OR AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `THE HAND SPEAKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let the left hand hang loosely beside the left knee, palm open and turned forward, fingers pointing down toward the floor. That's the giving hand. Raise the right hand to about shoulder height, palm facing forward, fingers up, relaxed rather than stiff. That's the hand that says do not fear. Hold both, and breathe slowly. If a worry comes to mind, let it sit in front of the raised palm. Don't argue with it. Just let it meet the hand. If you pray, you can hold the gesture facing a home shrine. If you don't, simply let the two hands rest in their shapes and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, two you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the lowered palm that gives.

Your line: the mudras. Today, when someone near you is anxious, notice your own hands before you speak. Let them be open and unhurried, and see what they say before your words do. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Devotees meet abhaya and varada mudras on the images of deities in temples and home shrines; the raised open palm is read as "do not fear" and the lowered open palm as the giving of blessings.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: abhaya, fearlessness. Abhayam opens the list of divine qualities in Gita 16.

trapdoor: what you thought: the statue is waving hello.
what it means: abhaya mudra, the raised open palm that says do not be afraid, often paired with varada, the giving hand.
what a scholar hears: abhayam heads the list of daivi sampad, the divine qualities, at Bhagavad Gita 16.1.

Day 5 of the mudras block (1033–1039). Days 1033–1036 were not on disk when this was written; this day takes the iconographic angle (abhaya and varada on images) to avoid likely overlap with hand mudras used in practice. Check against 1033–1036 for repetition.
Gita 16.1 paraphrase: abhayam sattva-samshuddhir jnana-yoga-vyavasthitih, danam damash cha... Confirm the order given (fearlessness, purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge, giving, self-control).

Iconography claims to confirm: Nataraja's raised hand in abhaya; coins flowing from Lakshmi's lowered hand in some paintings; abhaya and varada also on Buddhist and Jain images (stated briefly as a shared vocabulary, not compared).
The two readings (promise of protection / invitation to the quality) are offered as interpretations, not attributed to a named school; a Keeper may want to attribute them.

Audit pass: practice fixed; it set the varada hand "palm up" on the knee with "fingers pointing down", which cannot both be true; varada is the open palm turned outward, fingers down. Days 1033–1036 are now on disk and were checked: no overlap with abhaya/varada.
